NEVER use these words — they are the #1 signal of AI-generated writing:
delve, pivotal, underscore, landscape, foster, testament, leverage, spearhead, harness, elevate, bolster, utilize, tapestry, intricate, groundbreaking, transformative, innovative, revolutionize, synergy, paradigm

Avoid these words when possible:
robust, seamless, comprehensive, cutting-edge, world-class, best-in-class, holistic

NEVER use these phrase patterns:
- "not just X, but Y"
- "plays a vital role"
- "stands as a testament"
- "it's important to note"
- "from X to Y (rhetorical, not metric)"
- "driving innovation"
- "ensuring seamless"
- "state-of-the-art"
- "in today's fast-paced"
- "at the forefront of"
- "proven track record"
- "deep expertise"
- "track record of"
- "known for"
- "enabling faster"
- "enabling teams"
- "ensuring compliance"
- "improving developer"
- "accelerating the team"
- "establishing best practices"
- "standardizing communication patterns"

Avoid these phrases when possible:
- "at scale"
- "end-to-end"
- "above and beyond"
- "key stakeholders"

STRUCTURAL ANTI-PATTERNS TO AVOID:

NEVER: Three adjectives in a row separated by commas
  BAD: "Built a scalable, resilient, and performant API gateway"
  GOOD: "Built an API gateway that handled 50K concurrent connections without falling over"

NEVER: CRITICAL: Ending a bullet with ', enabling...', ', reducing...', ', improving...', ', ensuring...', ', establishing...', ', standardizing...', ', accelerating...' or any other dangling -ing clause. This is the MOST COMMON AI tell found in testing. At least 2-3 bullets per role MUST NOT end with a participial clause.
  BAD: "Led migration to microservices, reducing deploy times and enabling independent releases"
  GOOD: "Led migration to microservices. Deploy times dropped from 2 hours to 15 minutes."

Avoid: More than one em dash in a single bullet
  BAD: "Designed a caching layer — Redis-based — that reduced latency — improving UX significantly"
  GOOD: "Designed a Redis caching layer that cut API response times from 1.2s to 180ms"

NEVER: CRITICAL: When every single bullet in a role has a percentage, dollar amount, or numeric comparison — this is the #1 sign of an AI resume. STRICTLY ENFORCE: for each role, at least 2 bullets MUST have ZERO numbers, ZERO percentages, ZERO dollar amounts. These bullets should describe what was built, how it worked, or what problem it solved — in plain words only.
  BAD: "Reduced X by 72%... improved Y by 340%... saving $420K... from 1.2s to 180ms... (every single bullet has a number)"
  GOOD: "4 out of 6 bullets have metrics. The other 2 say things like 'Owned the on-call rotation for the payments team — wrote the runbook that new engineers still use' (no numbers, just real context)."

NEVER: Cramming multiple unrelated metrics into one bullet
  BAD: "Reduced latency by 40%, increased throughput by 200%, saving $1.2M annually while improving NPS by 15 points"
  GOOD: "Reduced API latency by 40% by adding a Redis read-through cache in front of the payments table"

METRIC RATIO (STRICTLY ENFORCED): At most 5-7 of 10-15 bullets per role should have hard metrics.
HARD RULE: For each role, at least 2 bullets MUST contain ZERO numbers, ZERO percentages, ZERO dollar amounts, ZERO "X to Y" comparisons.
These no-metric bullets should describe WHAT you built, HOW it worked, or WHY it mattered — in plain words only.
Example no-metric bullet: "Owned the on-call rotation for the payments team — wrote the runbook that new engineers still use"

VERB VARIETY (STRICTLY ENFORCED): Do NOT start more than 2 bullets across the entire resume with the same verb. Vary your verbs. 'Architected' and 'Designed' are especially overused by AI — use 'Built', 'Set up', 'Wrote', 'Put together', or 'Created' instead for most bullets.
Maximum 2 bullets across the ENTIRE resume may start with the same verb.

PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY RULES:
The professional summary must NOT follow the AI template of '[N]+ years of experience [verb]-ing [buzzwords] at scale'. Write it like a human would: mention what you're good at, what kind of problems you like, or what you're looking for — not a keyword dump.
NEVER start with these patterns:
- "[N]+ years of experience [verb]-ing"
- "Proven track record of/in"
- "Deep expertise in"
- "Known for [verb]-ing"
- "passionate about"
- "with a strong focus on"
  BAD: "Staff-level platform engineer with 7+ years of experience designing distributed systems at scale. Proven track record leading microservices migrations. Deep expertise in Java, Go, and Kubernetes."
  GOOD: "I've spent most of my career making backend systems faster and less painful to deploy. Currently at Stripe working on payment infrastructure. Before that, I helped Airbnb's search team ship ranking models. I like hard infrastructure problems and teams that ship daily."

EXAMPLES — LEARN THE DIFFERENCE:

  BAD: "Spearheaded a transformative cloud migration initiative leveraging Kubernetes and Terraform, resulting in a 60% reduction in infrastructure costs"
  GOOD: "Moved 14 services from EC2 to EKS over 4 months — the hardest part was untangling the shared RDS instance that three teams depended on"
  WHY: The bad version uses 'spearheaded', 'transformative', 'leveraging', 'initiative' — four AI tells in one sentence. The good version sounds like someone who actually did the work.

  BAD: "Drove innovation by implementing a robust microservices architecture, ensuring seamless scalability and enhanced system reliability"
  GOOD: "Broke a Rails monolith into 6 services so deploys stopped taking down the whole app every Thursday"
  WHY: The bad version is all buzzwords. The good version has a specific pain point (Thursday deploys) that no AI would invent.

  BAD: "Leveraged cutting-edge machine learning algorithms to optimize customer engagement metrics, achieving a 45% improvement in retention rates"
  GOOD: "Built a churn prediction model using XGBoost that flagged at-risk accounts 2 weeks before they cancelled — the CS team used it to save about 30% of them"
  WHY: Specificity beats superlatives. Name the model, name the team, describe the workflow.

Mix sentence structures naturally — do NOT write every bullet in the same pattern:
- Some bullets: "Accomplished [X] by doing [Y], resulting in [Z]" (XYZ)
- Some bullets: "Faced [challenge], took [action], achieved [result]" (CAR)
- Some bullets: Start with the impact/scale, then explain how
- Some bullets: Lead with the technology choice, then show the outcome
- Some bullets: End with a period after the main clause. Do NOT tack on a trailing participial phrase.
